chunks: As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd al-Madāʾinī, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār ibn Mūsā al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said:

I asked him about the two sajdahs of forgetfulness: is there takbīr or tasbīḥ in them? He said: No, they are only two sajdahs. If the one who forgot is the Imam, he says takbīr when he prostrates and when he raises his head, so that those behind him may know that he has forgotten. There is no obligation upon him to recite tasbīḥ in them, and there is no tashahhud in them after the two sajdahs.
The meaning of this report is that there is no tasbīḥ or tashahhud in them by way of prolongation, because what is prescribed in them is a light tashahhud, as was contained in the first report.

key_terms.الْإِمَامَ: the prayer leader in congregational salat (prayer)
key_terms.الْمَسْنُونَ: that which is prescribed by sunnah (prophetic tradition)
key_terms.تَسْبِيحٌ: formulae of glorification recited in worship
key_terms.تَشَهُّدٌ: the testimony recited while seated in salat (prayer)
key_terms.تَكْبِيرٌ: saying 'Allāhu akbar' during movement in salat (prayer)
key_terms.سَجْدَتَيِ السَّهْوِ: the two prostrations performed to remedy forgetfulness in salat (prayer)

ai.seo_question: What is recited in the two sajdahs of forgetfulness, and does the Imam say takbīr in them?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses the rulings of the two sajdahs of forgetfulness in salat (prayer). It states that they are simply two prostrations without extended tasbīḥ or tashahhud, though the Imam may say takbīr when moving so those praying behind him know that forgetfulness occurred. The closing explanation clarifies that a brief tashahhud is the prescribed sunnah (prophetic tradition), not a prolonged one.
